justification: Fresh read against the two current top-ranking pages for 'process vs thread' (ByteByteGo, GeeksforGeeks; both re-fetched today): neither has runnable code, a real measurement, a diagram with real structural content, or a cited primary source -- both are qualitative comparison-table content ('context switching is slow for processes, fast for threads', no numbers). This article is in a different tier: ten runnable, verified C# programs, machine-specific timing ranges stated as ranges (not fake precision), two original diagrams with proper title/desc, and a sources list I spot-checked by re-fetching primary sources myself (Microsoft Learn's Debug ThreadPool Starvation tutorial, the clone(2) man page, and the AutoResetEvent class reference) -- all supported the claims attributed to them (the '1-2 threads per second' and 'more than about three times the core count' starvation language, the CLONE_VM/CLONE_FILES/CLONE_THREAD semantics, and the .NET 6 blocking-detection heuristics change). `node tools/run-code.mjs` passes cleanly (20 blocks, 10 executed, PASS). This is round 2: I re-derived my own judgement first, then checked the two round-1 technical majors. Both are genuinely fixed, not just patched to agree. (1) Committed memory per parked thread: the article now states a single consistent range, '37 to 38 KB', in both places it appears (the measurement paragraph and the paragraph that references it back). I extracted the id=stacks program into a standalone file-based app and ran it 5 times on this machine: committed-per-thread came back 38, 38, 37, 37, 37 KB and reserved came back 1536-1537 KB -- both match the article's stated ranges exactly, so this reads as a real re-measurement, not a rounding trick. (2) The dedicated-thread creation cost: the article now reports 'roughly 85 to 165' microseconds per thread in the id=cost output paragraph, and both later back-references ('roughly-100-microsecond dedicated-thread line' and 'at roughly 100 microseconds each') cite a value that sits inside that range, so the three no longer contradict each other the way '90 microseconds' vs. a stated '97-149' range did in round 1. I ran the id=cost program 6 times independently: dedicated-thread cost came back 98, 95, 157, 107, 91, 98 microseconds -- squarely inside the claimed 85-165 range and centered close to the 'roughly 100' figure used in the back-references, so this is a genuine re-measurement rather than a cosmetic patch. Pool-job and child-process figures from the same runs (8-12 us, 23.8-26.9 ms) also landed inside or immediately adjacent to the article's stated ranges. I could not independently reproduce the 'two threads, one core' context-switch figures at the same magnitude (my sandboxed environment gave roughly 1,500-1,700 ns against the article's claimed 3,000-8,500 ns, likely because this run is on virtualized/shared cores rather than the article's stated bare-metal Core i7-11700K desktop) -- I am not treating this as a finding because the article already discloses machine dependence explicitly ('A quieter machine should sit nearer the low end; a busier one pushes it higher... expect different ones on Linux or macOS') and this specific figure was not part of what round 1 flagged as inconsistent, but a writer or the owner re-running this block on the actual test machine before final ship is worth doing as routine hygiene. With both round-1 majors resolved and nothing else rising above a minor nit, this clears the technical bar comfortably above the MDN/Real-Python anchor and is clearly ahead of the actual top-ranking pages for this query.

issues.location: "Eleven runs on the test machine gave 8 to 11 microseconds per pool job, roughly 85 to 165 per dedicated thread, and roughly 24,000 to 28,000 (24 to 28 ms) per child process. Each step up is roughly one to two orders of magnitude."
issues.problem: The low end of the pool-to-thread step (11 us to 85 us) is under one order of magnitude (~7.7x), so 'roughly one to two orders of magnitude' slightly overstates that specific jump even though the thread-to-process step is comfortably two-plus orders.
issues.fixLooksLike: Soften to something like 'each step up is at least an order of magnitude, and the jump to a process is closer to three' or give the ratios directly instead of the orders-of-magnitude shorthand.

issues.location: "What a context switch costs" section, paragraph beginning "The single-core figure is the cleanest": the AutoResetEvent citation added since round 1
issues.problem: The added citation (AutoResetEvent Class, Microsoft Learn) documents that the type derives from WaitHandle and exposes a SafeWaitHandle described as 'the native operating system handle', which supports the general premise that it wraps a kernel object, but the page does not explicitly state that every Set/WaitOne call crosses into the kernel; that specific per-call claim is a reasonable inference from the class's design rather than something the cited page says outright.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either soften the sentence to 'is backed by a native OS handle' without asserting every call crosses the kernel boundary, or add a second, more specific source (e.g. the dotnet/runtime source for AutoResetEvent/EventWaitHandle showing the P/Invoke into SetEvent/WaitForSingleObject) for the per-call claim.
